entries.title: Grade 1 Ontario History: My Community, Special Places, and Stories from the Past
entries.contentBody: In grade 1, Ontario history begins with the child's own world: the community where they live. Students learn that a community is the group of people, buildings, and places near where they live, and that every community has a history, meaning a story of how things were in the past and how they changed. Students explore what makes their community special by looking at local landmarks, parks, schools, places of worship, and gathering places. They are introduced to famous Ontario landmarks such as the CN Tower in Toronto, Niagara Falls, and the Parliament Buildings in Ottawa on the border of Ontario, and they learn that landmarks are places that are important to many people. Students learn simple time words such as long ago, yesterday, today, and in the past, and they begin to place events in order, for example that grandparents were children before parents were children. They hear stories about the First Peoples of Ontario, including the Anishinaabe, the Haudenosaunee, and the Cree, and learn in simple terms that these nations have lived on this land for a very long time and still live here today. Students learn about caring for the land and for shared places. Families are a key source of history, and students interview family members or look at old photographs to find out about the past. The grade 1 goal is not memorizing dates but building the idea that today is connected to the past, that places hold stories, and that Ontario is home to many peoples with long histories.
entries.pedagogicalNotes: Keep concepts concrete and local. Young students confuse past, present, and future, so use clear anchors such as last year or when grandparents were small rather than dates. Build vocabulary such as community, landmark, past, and history through real photographs and a walk around the neighborhood. Avoid treating First Nations history as only long ago; explicitly connect it to the present. Common misconception: students think the past is black and white because old photographs are, so show color images of the past too. Scaffold with picture timelines and family story sharing.

exampleProblems.problem: Put these events in order from longest ago to most recent: your grandmother was a little girl, the CN Tower opened, you were born.
exampleProblems.solution: First your grandmother was a little girl, then the CN Tower opened in 1976, then you were born most recently.
exampleProblems.explanation: Timelines start with the event that happened earliest and move toward today. Since grandmother was a child before you were born and the tower was built before you were born, grandmother's childhood comes first.

exampleProblems.problem: Name one landmark in Ontario and explain why it is important to people.
exampleProblems.solution: Example: Niagara Falls is important because it is a huge natural wonder that people travel from all over the world to visit, and many families take trips there.
exampleProblems.explanation: A landmark is a place that is important or well known. Any valid Ontario landmark such as the CN Tower or Parliament Hill is acceptable if the student gives a reason about why people value the place.

exampleProblems.problem: Amir says that the First Peoples of Ontario only lived here in the past and are gone today. Is he right? Explain.
exampleProblems.solution: No, he is not right. The Anishinaabe, Haudenosaunee, and Cree peoples lived here long ago and still live in Ontario today.
exampleProblems.explanation: This checks the common misconception that Indigenous peoples belong only to the distant past. First Nations communities are part of Ontario now, in cities and in communities across the province.

entries.title: Grade 2 Ontario History: Changing Communities, Stories of the Land, and Simple Timelines
entries.contentBody: In grade 2, students build on the idea that communities change over time. They compare their community long ago and today, looking at how homes, transportation, shops, schools, and jobs have changed, for example from horse and wagon to cars, or from small trading posts to modern towns. Students learn that Ontario is a province, one of the ten provinces of Canada, with its own landscapes including the Great Lakes, forests, rivers, and cities. They continue learning about the First Peoples of Ontario: the Anishinaabe, the Haudenosaunee, and the Cree. In age-appropriate terms students learn that these nations have their own languages, stories, and traditions; that many place names in Ontario come from Indigenous languages, such as Toronto from a Haudenosaunee word for a meeting place on the water; and that First Nations peoples cared for the land through practices such as fishing, farming the Three Sisters crops of corn, beans, and squash, and traveling by canoe along rivers and lakes. Students learn why Niagara Falls, the CN Tower, and Parliament Hill matter, and how a place can be important to different groups of people for different reasons. They use simple timelines with dates and pictures to order events in their family and community, and they learn that a timeline shows events in the order they happened. The focus is on change and continuity: some things in Ontario look very different now, and some things, such as the land and waterways, have shaped life for hundreds of years.
entries.pedagogicalNotes: Use then-and-now photo comparisons of the same local street or building; students need concrete evidence to grasp change over time. Scaffold timelines with picture cards before introducing numerals. Misconceptions: students may think life long ago was the same everywhere in Ontario, so contrast rural, northern, and city communities. Also counter the idea that First Nations history is one single culture; emphasize that the Anishinaabe, Haudenosaunee, and Cree are distinct peoples. Oral history and storytelling fit this grade well; keep interview tasks simple with sentence stems.

exampleProblems.problem: Look at two pictures of the same Ontario town: one shows a dirt road with a horse and wagon in 1900, the other shows the same street with cars and a bus today. Name two things that changed.
exampleProblems.solution: The road went from dirt to paved, and transportation changed from a horse and wagon to cars and buses.
exampleProblems.explanation: Students compare evidence from two points in time. Any two valid changes such as taller buildings, different clothing, or new shops earn credit, as long as they come from the pictures.

exampleProblems.problem: Why is a canoe a very important invention for the First Peoples of Ontario?
exampleProblems.solution: Because Ontario has many lakes and rivers, the canoe let people travel, trade, and fish along the waterways before roads existed.
exampleProblems.explanation: Geography shapes how people live. The canoe fit the Ontario landscape of the Great Lakes and rivers, making travel and carrying goods possible.

exampleProblems.problem: Make a simple timeline for these events and put them in order: your great-grandparents got married, your parent was born, your school was built, you started grade 2.
exampleProblems.solution: Great-grandparents got married, then your parent was born, then your school was built, then you started grade 2.
exampleProblems.explanation: A timeline orders events from earliest to latest. Students can verify the order by thinking about who was alive when and what they can ask family members about.

entries.title: Grade 3 Ontario History: First Nations of Ontario, the Land, and Early Communities
entries.contentBody: In grade 3, Ontario history turns to the First Nations peoples of Ontario and the relationship between people and the land. Students study the Anishinaabe, including the Ojibwe, Odawa, and Potawatomi, the Haudenosaunee also called the Iroquois or Six Nations, and the Cree of northern Ontario. They learn where these peoples traditionally lived: the Haudenosaunee in the south near the lower Great Lakes, the Anishinaabe around the Great Lakes and the northern forests, and the Cree across the far north. Students learn about traditional ways of life shaped by the land and seasons, including hunting, fishing, gathering wild rice, farming corn beans and squash, and traveling by birchbark canoe along the Great Lakes and river routes. They learn about the longhouse as a Haudenosaunee home and about the importance of the Great Law of Peace as an early agreement among nations about how to live together and make decisions. Students learn about the Three Sisters planting, the use of natural resources such as cedar, birchbark, and sweetgrass, and about stories and oral traditions that teach values and knowledge across generations. They begin to understand that Ontario's land and waterways, especially the Great Lakes, shaped where people lived and how they traded and traveled. Students also meet early European visitors and the beginnings of contact and trade, learning that First Nations were skilled partners in trade and knew the land well. Respect for the land and for Indigenous knowledge, including treaties and the idea of sharing and caring for the land, runs through the grade.
entries.pedagogicalNotes: Teach each nation separately so students see Anishinaabe, Haudenosaunee, and Cree as distinct peoples with distinct homes, languages, and practices, not one generic First Nations culture. Use maps and hands-on artifacts or images such as birchbark canoes and longhouses. Misconception: that Indigenous peoples did not farm; explicitly teach the Three Sisters agriculture of the Haudenosaunee. Avoid past-only framing: include present-day communities such as Six Nations of the Grand River. Scaffold map work with color coding by nation, and set respectful discussion norms for learning about other cultures.

exampleProblems.problem: Match each First Nation to where it traditionally lived: Anishinaabe, Haudenosaunee, Cree. Choices: northern Ontario, around the Great Lakes and northern forests, southern Ontario near the lower Great Lakes.
exampleProblems.solution: Cree in northern Ontario, Anishinaabe around the Great Lakes and northern forests, Haudenosaunee in southern Ontario near the lower Great Lakes.
exampleProblems.explanation: Each nation's homeland matched its environment and way of life. Reading the map of Ontario and matching geography to peoples builds the link between land and culture.

exampleProblems.problem: What are the Three Sisters and why were they important to the Haudenosaunee?
exampleProblems.solution: The Three Sisters are corn, beans, and squash, grown together in one plot. They were important because they provided a healthy, reliable food supply.
exampleProblems.explanation: The crops help each other grow: corn gives a stalk for beans to climb, beans add nutrients to the soil, and squash leaves shade the ground. This is an example of Indigenous knowledge of farming.

exampleProblems.problem: Kai says that First Nations peoples did not really use the land and just wandered around. Using what you learned, explain why he is wrong.
exampleProblems.solution: He is wrong because First Nations peoples farmed corn, beans, and squash, fished the Great Lakes, hunted with the seasons, built villages and longhouses, and used canoes to travel and trade. They managed the land carefully for thousands of years.
exampleProblems.explanation: Evidence of farming, permanent villages like longhouses, and trade routes shows deliberate, skilled use of the land. Answers should cite at least two specific practices.

entries.title: Grade 4 Ontario History: Early Ontario, Explorers, Fur Trade Beginnings, and the Land
entries.contentBody: In grade 4, students begin the story of early Ontario: the land and its First Nations peoples, the arrival of French explorers and traders, and the early settlements that grew along the waterways. They learn how Ontario's geography, especially the Great Lakes, the St. Lawrence River, and the network of rivers and lakes, made travel, trade, and settlement possible. Students study early European exploration of the region, learning that French explorers and missionaries traveled through the Great Lakes in the 1600s and met First Nations peoples who were essential partners, guides, and traders. They begin learning about the fur trade in simple terms: European traders wanted animal pelts especially beaver furs to make hats in Europe, and First Nations trappers traded furs for metal tools, cloth, and other goods. Students learn how trading posts and early forts, which later became Ontario towns, were placed along lakes and rivers because water was the highway of the time. They learn what daily life was like for early settlers and for First Nations families, how homes were built from local materials, and how people depended on the seasons and the land. Topics such as Niagara Falls and the importance of waterways for power and transport connect back to the landmark study of earlier grades. Students develop skills with maps, simple timelines showing the 1600s and 1700s, and sources such as paintings and early written accounts. The grade emphasizes two big ideas: the land shaped history in Ontario, and history in Ontario has always involved many peoples living, trading, and working together.
entries.pedagogicalNotes: Anchor everything to waterways: have students trace travel routes on a map and see that highways did not exist, so rivers and lakes determined where people went and settled. Keep the fur trade concrete with the beaver hat connection and trade goods. Misconceptions: students think explorers discovered an empty land; stress that millions of people already lived here and that exploration depended on First Nations knowledge and partnership. Another misconception is that history only happens in wars and governments; use daily life and trade as the entry point. Scaffold vocabulary such as pelt, trade, voyageur, and settlement with images.

exampleProblems.problem: Why were most early trading posts and settlements in Ontario built next to lakes and rivers?
exampleProblems.solution: Because rivers and lakes were the highways of the time. Canoes and boats carried people, furs, and goods, so settlements grew where the water routes met.
exampleProblems.explanation: Before roads and railways, water was the fastest and easiest way to travel and move heavy loads like bundles of furs. Geography therefore decided where towns began.

exampleProblems.problem: Explain why beaver furs were so valuable to European traders in the 1600s and 1700s.
exampleProblems.solution: In Europe, beaver fur was used to make felt hats, which were very fashionable and expensive. Traders could sell the furs for a lot of money, so they came to Ontario to get them.
exampleProblems.explanation: The fur trade existed because of demand far away. Students see that something common in Ontario became valuable because of what it could become in another part of the world.

exampleProblems.problem: Two students discuss a painting of French voyageurs in a canoe trading with an Anishinaabe family. One says, 'The French taught the First Nations everything.' Is this a good reading of the evidence? What actually made the trade work?
exampleProblems.solution: No. The trade worked because both sides had skills and goods the other needed: First Nations peoples knew the land, trapped furs, and traveled by canoe, while the French offered metal tools, cloth, and other goods. It was a partnership, not one side teaching the other everything.
exampleProblems.explanation: Primary source images show canoes, routes, and goods that only worked with First Nations knowledge of the waterways. Fair trade relationships and mutual dependence, not one-sided instruction, powered the fur trade.

entries.title: Grade 5 Ontario History: New France, the Fur Trade, and Early Life in the Ontario Region
entries.contentBody: In grade 5, students study New France and the fur trade in the lands that would become Ontario. They learn that France built a North American colony called New France along the St. Lawrence River, and that French explorers, missionaries, and fur traders pushed west through the Great Lakes into the Ontario region in the 1600s and 1700s. Key figures such as Samuel de Champlain, who traveled the Great Lakes and made alliances with First Nations, and Étienne Brûlé, one of the first Europeans to live among First Nations peoples in Ontario, appear in the story. Students learn how the fur trade actually worked: the chain of trade from Indigenous trappers to voyageurs who paddled huge canoes of furs to Montreal and Quebec, the role of trading posts like those that grew into Ontario towns, and the important partnership between French traders and First Nations allies such as the Huron-Wendat and the Anishinaabe. They learn about daily life in New France, including the seigneurial system of farming along the St. Lawrence, the Catholic missions, and the coureurs de bois who traveled the interior. Students also study the growing rivalry between France and Britain for control of the fur trade and the land, which sets up the conflict that ends with the British taking New France in 1760. Geography remains central: students use maps to trace the Great Lakes fur trade routes and understand why controlling waterways meant controlling trade. Skills developed include reading simple primary source accounts, placing events on a century timeline, and comparing the viewpoints of French, British, and First Nations participants in the same events.
entries.pedagogicalNotes: Build the fur trade as a system students can trace: trapping, trading, canoe transport, markets in Europe. Use maps repeatedly so students internalize that the Great Lakes network was the infrastructure of the era. Misconceptions: students assume French traders dominated or rescued First Nations; repeatedly frame trade as partnership and alliance, since French survival depended on First Nations knowledge. Distinguish Champlain and Brule roles and avoid an events-only story; include daily life and the seigneurial system for social history. Scaffold primary sources with glossed vocabulary and guided questions about who wrote the account and why. Prepare for later grades by naming the France-Britain rivalry without requiring details of the Seven Years' War.

exampleProblems.problem: Describe the journey of a beaver pelt from an Anishinaabe trapper to a hatter in Europe.
exampleProblems.solution: The trapper caught the beaver and prepared the pelt, traded it at a trading post for goods like metal tools and cloth, voyageurs carried bundles of furs by canoe to Montreal and then across the ocean, and in Europe the fur was made into a felt hat.
exampleProblems.explanation: The fur trade was a chain linking people across continents. Each step depended on the one before it, and First Nations trappers were the essential first link.

exampleProblems.problem: Why did Samuel de Champlain make alliances with First Nations nations such as the Huron-Wendat?
exampleProblems.solution: Because the French needed allies for the fur trade and for survival and exploration in unfamiliar territory. The alliances gave the French furs, food, guides, and military support.
exampleProblems.explanation: Alliances were practical partnerships. First Nations groups also gained trade goods and allies in their own conflicts, so both sides had reasons to cooperate.

exampleProblems.problem: A student says, 'The French came to Ontario and took over the land right away.' Use what you know about the 1600s fur trade to correct this statement.
exampleProblems.solution: The French did not take over Ontario. They came mainly to trade for furs, and they relied on First Nations partners and permission to live and travel in the region. French control was limited to trading posts and missions, and much of the fur trade network was run in cooperation with First Nations peoples until the British conquest of 1760.
exampleProblems.explanation: Mastery requires knowing that French presence was small and partnership-based, that the fur trade, not settlement, drove French interest in the Ontario region, and that the balance of power changed only after the British victory over New France.

entries.title: Grade 6 Ontario History: New France and the Great Lakes Fur Trade
entries.contentBody: In grade 6, students study New France and the fur trade in depth, tracing how France's colony shaped the lands that became Ontario. They learn the structure of New France: its government under a governor and intendant sent from France, the seigneurial system of long farm strips along the St. Lawrence, the Catholic Church's role in missions and schools, and daily life for habitant farmers, merchants, soldiers, and enslaved and indentured people. Students map the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence as the trade highway of North America and follow the fur trade system end to end: First Nations trappers supplied beaver and other pelts; trading posts and forts such as those at Frontenac and Michilimackinac connected the interior to Montreal; voyageurs paddled enormous canoes loaded with fur bundles; and European markets turned beaver felt into hats. Students learn that the trade was a partnership: French traders depended on First Nations knowledge, labor, and alliances, especially with the Huron-Wendat and later the Anishinaabe and other nations, and that competition over trade routes drew nations into wider conflicts. Key figures include Champlain, the coureurs de bois, and missionary explorers. Students also study the imperial rivalry between France and Britain, the events leading to the fall of New France in 1760, and the Royal Proclamation of 1763 that reorganized the territory. Skills include reading maps of trade routes, analyzing artifacts such as trade goods and canoes, and comparing the perspectives of French officials, traders, and First Nations partners. The big ideas are that economics and geography drove history in this region, and that Indigenous peoples were central agents in the story, not bystanders.
entries.pedagogicalNotes: Teach the fur trade as an economic system students can diagram end to end, since abstract detail alone does not stick at this level. Revisit the map often: students should be able to explain why Montreal, the Great Lakes, and portage routes mattered. Misconceptions: that the French owned the land they traded on; clarify that trade operated with First Nations consent and that the Proclamation of 1763 acknowledged Indigenous land rights. Also counter the myth of the empty land and the idea of a single First Nations culture. Scaffold with trade-simulation activities and glossed primary sources; prepare students for the Loyalist and War of 1812 topics ahead by naming the 1763 transfer of power to Britain without overloading detail.

exampleProblems.problem: Explain why the beaver pelt trade made France interested in the Great Lakes region when so few French farmers lived there.
exampleProblems.solution: Because beaver fur was extremely valuable in Europe and the Great Lakes region was rich in beaver. A few trading posts and partnerships with First Nations trappers could produce enormous profits without large-scale settlement.
exampleProblems.explanation: Economic demand, not farming, drove French expansion into Ontario. The waterways made transporting furs cheap, so trading posts along the Great Lakes served the trade.

exampleProblems.problem: Name two ways First Nations peoples were essential to the success of the fur trade.
exampleProblems.solution: They trapped and prepared the furs that supplied the trade, and they provided knowledge of the land, water routes, and survival skills, along with birchbark canoes to carry goods. They also set the terms of trade at posts and made alliances with the French.
exampleProblems.explanation: Without Indigenous labor and expertise the trade could not operate. Students should see First Nations peoples as skilled partners and decision-makers in the trade network.

exampleProblems.problem: A textbook says the French 'took control of Ontario' during the fur trade era. Using evidence about trade posts, alliances, and population, evaluate this claim.
exampleProblems.solution: The claim is misleading. The French had only small trading posts and missions in the Ontario region, not farms or towns like along the St. Lawrence. Trade ran through partnerships with First Nations nations who controlled their own territories. Real French settlement was concentrated in the St. Lawrence valley, and even that came under British control after 1760.
exampleProblems.explanation: Strong answers distinguish trade influence from political control and cite evidence such as the small French population, the location of posts, and the continuing autonomy of First Nations allies.

entries.title: Grade 7 Ontario History: The United Empire Loyalists and the Founding of Upper Canada
entries.contentBody: In grade 7, students learn how Ontario became a British colony shaped by the United Empire Loyalists. After the American Revolution ended in 1783, tens of thousands of Loyalists, people who had stayed loyal to the British Crown and lost their property and rights in the new United States, moved north into British North America. Many settled along the St. Lawrence River, the Bay of Quinte, and the Niagara Peninsula, and some Black Loyalists and freed or enslaved people of African descent also arrived, including communities that later settled in places like Oro and Buxton. Students learn that the British government granted land to Loyalists, created the new colony of Upper Canada in 1791 through the Constitutional Act, and set up a government with an appointed governor, an appointed Legislative Council, and an elected Legislative Assembly. Upper Canada's first lieutenant-governor, John Graves Simcoe, promoted British institutions such as the rule of law, English common law, and even plans to limit slavery, and he founded the town of York in 1793, which later became Toronto. Students study life in a pioneer Loyalist township: clearing forests, building log homes, farming, and the difficult first winters, as well as the experiences of Indigenous nations whose lands were negotiated or taken through treaties in this period. Key themes include immigration and its causes, the meeting of Loyalist, Indigenous, and French-speaking communities, and the beginnings of Ontario's political institutions. Students compare why people moved, how land was granted, and how the new colony's society was organized by class and background.
entries.pedagogicalNotes: Use cause-and-effect framing throughout: the American Revolution caused the Loyalist migration, which caused the creation of Upper Canada. Concrete artifacts such as land grant documents and pioneer journals make the settlement story real. Misconceptions: students assume Loyalists were all wealthy British soldiers; in fact they included farmers, formerly enslaved Black people, and Indigenous allies such as the Mohawks of the Bay of Quinte. Another misconception is that the land was empty before Loyalists arrived; teach the treaties and displacement of First Nations alongside settlement. Scaffold with migration maps and a class comparison chart of reasons for moving. Link forward to the War of 1812 by noting that many Loyalist settlers still feared American invasion.

exampleProblems.problem: Why did the United Empire Loyalists leave the United States after 1783?
exampleProblems.solution: Because they had remained loyal to Britain during the American Revolution and were persecuted in the new United States. They lost property, rights, and safety, so the British government offered them free land and support in what became Upper Canada.
exampleProblems.explanation: Migration has causes: political loyalty, loss, and the pull of new land and British protection all pushed and pulled the Loyalists north.

exampleProblems.problem: What did the Constitutional Act of 1791 create, and why does it matter for Ontario's history?
exampleProblems.solution: It split Quebec into Upper Canada and Lower Canada and gave Upper Canada its own government with a governor, an appointed council, and an elected assembly. It matters because this is where Ontario begins as a distinct colony with its own political institutions.
exampleProblems.explanation: This act established the framework of government that reformers like Baldwin and LaFontaine would later fight to make responsible in the 1840s.

exampleProblems.problem: Priya says, 'Everyone in Upper Canada was a Loyalist.' Using what you know about the colony's population, correct her statement.
exampleProblems.solution: Not everyone was a Loyalist. Upper Canada also included First Nations peoples whose nations had lived there for thousands of years and who had made treaties with the Crown, French-speaking communities, later immigrants from Britain and elsewhere, and enslaved and free Black residents, including Black Loyalists. The colony was more diverse than a single group.
exampleProblems.explanation: Good answers name at least two non-Loyalist groups and recognize that First Nations presence long predated the colony. Students should see Upper Canada as a layered society.

entries.title: Grade 8 Ontario History: The War of 1812 and the Rebellion of 1837 in Upper Canada
entries.contentBody: In grade 8, students study two conflicts that shaped Upper Canada: the War of 1812 and the Rebellion of 1837. For the War of 1812, they learn that the United States declared war on Britain over issues such as trade restrictions, British support for First Nations resistance to American expansion, and American desire for territory. Upper Canada became a battleground, and students follow key events such as the battles of Queenston Heights where Isaac Brock died, the burning of York in 1813, battles on the Great Lakes, and the successful defense of the colony. They learn that the defense of Upper Canada depended on a coalition of British soldiers, Canadian militia including many Loyalist settlers, and crucial First Nations allies led by figures such as Tecumseh, whose efforts were vital in the western campaigns. The war ended with the Treaty of Ghent in 1814, changing little on the map but strengthening Upper Canada's identity and its ties to Britain and reinforcing Indigenous alliances, though First Nations peoples gained little from the peace. Students then study the Rebellion of 1837 in Upper Canada, a revolt led by William Lyon Mackenzie against the ruling elite called the Family Compact, who controlled the government, land, and jobs. They learn why many settlers were angry: unfair land grants, economic depression, lack of responsible government, and a legislative assembly with little power. The rebellion failed quickly, and its legacy was major: the British government sent Lord Durham to investigate, his report recommended responsible government and uniting the Canadas, leading to the Act of Union in 1841. Students analyze causes and consequences, distinguish the two conflicts, and evaluate how defeat and reform changed politics in Upper Canada.
entries.pedagogicalNotes: Keep the two conflicts clearly separated: 1812 is an American invasion and the 1837 rebellion is an internal political revolt. Cause-and-effect chains are the core skill. Misconceptions: students believe the War of 1812 was a Canadian victory in the sense of conquest; stress that Upper Canada survived the invasion and why that mattered to identity, while the treaty changed almost nothing. For 1837, students may assume the rebellion was a popular revolution; explain it was a limited uprising and that reform came through political change afterward. Use battle maps and Mackenzie's writings; scaffold with a Venn diagram comparing the wars. Highlight First Nations contributions in 1812 and their disappointment afterward to keep Indigenous agency visible.

exampleProblems.problem: Give two reasons the United States declared war on Britain in 1812 and explain how Upper Canada was affected.
exampleProblems.solution: Reasons included British interference with American trade and shipping during the Napoleonic Wars, and British support for First Nations resisting American settlement. Upper Canada became a battlefield, with attacks, battles, and the burning of York, and its settlers had to defend the colony.
exampleProblems.explanation: The war's causes were about empire and expansion far from Upper Canada, but the colony bore the fighting on the ground.

exampleProblems.problem: Explain how First Nations allies, including Tecumseh's confederacy, were important to the defense of Upper Canada in the War of 1812.
exampleProblems.solution: First Nations warriors provided essential military support, knowledge of the land, and victories in the western campaigns that delayed and weakened American attacks. Leaders like Tecumseh built alliances and fought alongside British and Canadian forces.
exampleProblems.explanation: Without this alliance the defense of Upper Canada would have been much harder. Students should note that despite their contributions, First Nations nations were not included in the peace and lost their goal of an independent homeland in the region.

exampleProblems.problem: Compare the causes of the War of 1812 and the Rebellion of 1837. How were they different kinds of conflict?
exampleProblems.solution: The War of 1812 was an external war started by the United States against Britain, fought on Upper Canadian soil with British, Canadian, and First Nations forces defending the colony. The Rebellion of 1837 was an internal revolt of Upper Canadian reformers led by Mackenzie against the local Family Compact elite over political unfairness and hard times. The first was about invasion and empire; the second was about who should govern the colony.
exampleProblems.explanation: One conflict is a war between countries; the other is a civil uprising within a colony. The rebellion's failure led to Durham's report and eventually responsible government, while the war's outcome was survival and a stronger colonial identity.

entries.title: Grade 9 Ontario History: Baldwin, LaFontaine, and Responsible Government
entries.contentBody: In grade 9, students study the reform movement that brought responsible government to the Canadas, focusing on Robert Baldwin and Louis-Hippolyte LaFontaine and the political struggles of the 1840s. They learn what responsible government means: the idea that the elected assembly, not the appointed governor, should control the government, and that ministers must have the support of the elected representatives and can be voted out of power. Students first trace the road to reform: the discontent behind the Rebellions of 1837 in both Upper and Lower Canada, Lord Durham's 1839 report that recommended uniting the Canadas and granting responsible government, and the Act of Union in 1841 that merged Upper and Lower Canada into the Province of Canada. They learn how Baldwin, an Upper Canada reformer, and LaFontaine, a Lower Canada French-Canadian leader, formed an unlikely and historic partnership across linguistic and cultural lines, building a coalition that demanded an end to rule by the appointed governor and the old ruling elites, the Family Compact in Upper Canada and the Chateau Clique in Lower Canada. Students follow their political victories, including LaFontaine's first government and Baldwin's reforms such as the municipal reform that created local self-government in Canada West, and the achievement of responsible government in 1848 when the governor accepted that ministers must hold the confidence of the assembly. Students examine how French-language rights and Catholic school protections became part of this new politics, and how Baldwin and LaFontaine's cooperation laid groundwork for a system in which English and French Canadians governed together. Skills include analyzing political cartoons and letters, evaluating the roles of individuals and institutions, and understanding compromise as a political tool.
entries.pedagogicalNotes: The concept of responsible government is abstract; make it concrete with a classroom analogy such as a principal who must follow what the elected student council decides. The Baldwin-LaFontaine partnership is the emotional heart of the topic: students often assume English and French politicians were always enemies, so highlight this alliance explicitly. Misconceptions: that responsible government meant independence from Britain, or that the 1837 rebellions directly succeeded; clarify that change came by negotiation and election afterward, and that Canada remained British until Confederation. Link Durham's report to the Act of Union and 1848 reforms in a clear cause chain. Scaffold vocabulary: ministry, confidence of the house, franchise, coalition.

exampleProblems.problem: Define responsible government in your own words and explain why the elected assembly wanted it.
exampleProblems.solution: Responsible government means the government must answer to the elected assembly rather than the appointed governor, and ministers must keep the support of the majority of elected members. The assembly wanted it so that the people's elected representatives, not a governor sent from Britain, actually decided laws and spending.
exampleProblems.explanation: This flips control from appointed elites to elected officials. It is a foundation of how Ontario and Canada are governed today.

exampleProblems.problem: Why was the partnership between Robert Baldwin and Louis-Hippolyte LaFontaine significant?
exampleProblems.solution: Because it united English-speaking reformers from Canada West and French-speaking reformers from Canada East in a common cause. Together they had enough support to win elections and show that responsible government could work across linguistic lines, which was essential since the Province of Canada contained both communities.
exampleProblems.explanation: Their coalition turned two separate reform movements into a majority program. It also set a precedent for English and French cooperation in Canadian politics.

exampleProblems.problem: A student argues, 'The rebellions of 1837 succeeded because Canada became a democracy right after.' Evaluate this claim using the sequence of events up to 1848.
exampleProblems.solution: The claim is wrong. The rebellions were defeated militarily in 1837. What changed was the response: Durham's report recommended uniting the Canadas and responsible government, the Act of Union passed in 1840, and reformers like Baldwin and LaFontaine then won responsible government through elections and negotiation, achieved in 1848. Reform came through politics after the rebellions failed, not from the uprisings themselves.
exampleProblems.explanation: Students must get the chronology and causation right: rebellion, defeat, investigation, union, reform coalition, responsible government. Confusing correlation with direct cause is the main error to avoid.

entries.title: Grade 10 Ontario History: Railways, Industrialization, and Ontario's Entry into Confederation
entries.contentBody: In grade 10, students study the economic and political transformation that created modern Ontario: railways and industrialization, and Confederation in 1867. They learn how the Province of Canada industrialized in the mid-1800s, with railways such as the Grand Trunk Railway linking towns, moving farm goods and raw materials to markets, and pulling people into growing cities. Students explore how new technologies such as the steam engine, the telegraph, and mechanized mills changed work from farms and small workshops to factories in towns like Toronto, Hamilton, and Ottawa, and how immigration from Britain and elsewhere supplied labor for railways and mills. They learn the social effects of industrialization: the growth of cities, factory working conditions, the roles of women and children in the workforce, and the beginnings of labor organization. Students then study the movement toward Confederation. They examine why the British North American colonies considered uniting: deadlock between Canada West and Canada East in the Province of Canada, fear of American expansion especially after the Civil War and threats like the Fenian raids, the need for a railway to tie the colonies together and open the west, and British pressure for the colonies to manage their own defense. Key figures include John A. Macdonald of Canada West, George-Étienne Cartier of Canada East, and other Fathers of Confederation. Students follow the Charlottetown and Quebec Conferences of 1864 and the British North America Act of 1867, which created the Dominion of Canada with Ontario as one of the four founding provinces, with its capital at Toronto and then Ottawa as the national capital. Students also consider Indigenous nations and the treaties of this era, and evaluate Confederation's promises and limits. Skills include weighing economic and political causes, reading political speeches and maps, and assessing how decisions in the 1860s still shape Ontario today.
entries.pedagogicalNotes: Balance the political story of Confederation with the economic story of railways and industry so students see that both drove change. Use maps of rail lines and conference locations; the deadlock of the double majority and the representation-by-population dispute are abstract and need careful scaffolding. Misconceptions: that Confederation was only about Canadian nationalism, or that it was inevitable; stress concrete motives like railway economics, American threat, and political deadlock. Also the misconception that Confederation created a fully independent Canada; Britain still controlled foreign affairs. Include perspectives of Indigenous peoples, whose treaties and land rights were often ignored or renegotiated on colonial terms. Build essay-level skills by having students weigh multiple causes rather than naming a single one.

exampleProblems.problem: Give two ways the railway changed life and the economy in Ontario in the mid-1800s.
exampleProblems.solution: Railways carried farm products and manufactured goods to distant markets, and they moved people and immigrants into towns, helping cities like Toronto and Hamilton grow. They also created factory jobs and linked Ontario towns together, so trade no longer depended only on rivers and roads.
exampleProblems.explanation: Transportation drives economic change. Just as rivers guided settlement earlier, railways reshaped where people lived and worked in industrial Ontario.

exampleProblems.problem: Explain two reasons the British North American colonies agreed to form Confederation in 1867.
exampleProblems.solution: First, political deadlock in the Province of Canada made government unstable and the colonies wanted a new system. Second, the colonies faced outside threats like the Fenian raids and feared American expansion after the U.S. Civil War, and they needed shared defense and a railway to the west. Economic needs and British encouragement also mattered.
exampleProblems.explanation: Confederation had multiple causes working together. Strong answers name at least two and connect each to a specific problem the colonies faced in the 1860s.

exampleProblems.problem: Evaluate the statement: 'Confederation in 1867 made Canada an independent country.' Use at least two pieces of evidence.
exampleProblems.solution: The statement is inaccurate. In 1867 the BNA Act created a self-governing Dominion, but Britain still controlled Canada's foreign affairs and could amend the constitution, and the highest court of appeal was in Britain. Canada only gained full legislative independence later with the Statute of Westminster in 1931 and patriation of the constitution in 1982. Confederation was a major step toward independence but not independence itself.
exampleProblems.explanation: Students must distinguish self-government from full sovereignty and date the later steps correctly. The best answers also note that Indigenous nations were not consulted as equal parties and were drawn into treaties under Crown authority, which complicates any simple story of national independence.

entries.title: Grade 11 Ontario History: The First World War and Ontario's Home Front
entries.contentBody: At the Grade 11 level students learn how the First World War from 1914 to 1918 reshaped Ontario society and politics. Ontario in 1914 was a province of farms, growing industrial cities, and a strong British identity, and students see how the war accelerated industrialization, government regulation, and social change. Core topics include enlistment and the Canadian Corps, with Ontario recruits serving in major battles such as Ypres, the Somme, Vimy Ridge, and Passchendaele, and the 1917 conscription crisis that split English-speaking Ontario, which largely supported the Military Service Act, from French-speaking Canada, which largely opposed it. Students examine the home front in detail: Victory Bond campaigns and patriotic fundraising, war production in Toronto munitions plants and Hamilton steel mills, censorship under the War Measures Act, price controls, and the internment of several thousand designated enemy aliens, many of them Ukrainian and other immigrants from Austria-Hungary. They study women's expanding roles in factories, nursing, and voluntary organizations, and connect wartime service to the granting of women's provincial suffrage in 1918 and to the 1917 provincial prohibition referendum, which led to the later creation of the Liquor Control Board of Ontario. Students also consider the contributions of First Nations soldiers who volunteered in large numbers even though they were exempt from conscription, and the unequal veterans' benefits they later received. The war's end brings the 1918 influenza pandemic, demobilization, labour unrest with echoes of the 1919 Winnipeg General Strike in Ontario cities, and a difficult economic readjustment. Throughout the unit students practice reading primary sources such as newspaper editorials, propaganda posters, and soldiers' letters, and they learn to separate the long-term causes of the war from its consequences for Ontario.
entries.pedagogicalNotes: Scaffold the unit with a timeline from 1914 to 1921 so students can see cause and effect. Common misconceptions: students assume all Canadians supported conscription, or that the war was experienced the same way in cities, farming communities, and Indigenous communities. Use local enlistment records and propaganda posters before assigning textbook readings, and always distinguish the European battle narrative from the Ontario home-front narrative.

exampleProblems.problem: Give two ways the First World War changed daily life for people living in Ontario cities between 1914 and 1918.
exampleProblems.solution: Any two of: factory work shifted to war production such as shells, explosives, and steel; consumer goods like sugar and flour were scarce and prices rose, so the government imposed price controls; families had members serving overseas, so women took paid industrial jobs; patriotic activities such as buying Victory Bonds and knitting for soldiers became part of ordinary life; newspapers were censored and enemy aliens faced restrictions and internment.
exampleProblems.explanation: This is an easy recall and connection question. Students should answer with specific home-front examples rather than battles, which shows they understand that the war affected Ontario communities even far from the fighting.

exampleProblems.problem: Explain why the 1917 conscription debate created a deep division between English-speaking Ontario and French-speaking Canada.
exampleProblems.solution: By 1916 voluntary enlistment had fallen and the government of Robert Borden introduced the Military Service Act in 1917 to draft men for overseas service. English-speaking Ontario, with strong British loyalty and heavy casualties at battles like the Somme, largely saw conscription as a duty to the empire. French-speaking Canadians, led by Henri Bourassa and Quebec politicians, argued that the war was a British imperial matter and that conscription violated their rights. Ontario voted overwhelmingly for Borden's Union government in the 1917 election, while Quebec rejected it, leaving a political and linguistic rift that lasted for decades.
exampleProblems.explanation: The question asks for an explanation, not just a description. A strong answer links the policy (the Military Service Act) to the different identities and arguments in each region, and shows how the 1917 election made the division visible.

exampleProblems.problem: Using the idea of the home front, assess whether the First World War was a turning point for women in Ontario. Support your answer with two pieces of evidence.
exampleProblems.solution: A strong answer argues it was a turning point but an incomplete one. Evidence one: women entered munitions factories and other industrial jobs in large numbers, proving they could do work previously reserved for men and gaining economic independence. Evidence two: women's wartime service strengthened the case for political rights, and Ontario granted women the provincial vote in 1918, followed by the first women elected to the Ontario legislature in 1919. A balanced conclusion notes that many women were pushed out of industrial jobs when soldiers returned, and that full equality in pay and opportunity was still far away.
exampleProblems.explanation: This hard question requires a judgement supported by evidence. Students learn to build an argument with a clear claim, specific evidence, and a counter-consideration, which is the core skill of historical argumentation at this level.

entries.title: Grade 12 Ontario History: The Great Depression and the Crisis of the 1930s
entries.contentBody: At the Grade 12 level students study how the Great Depression affected Ontario from the stock market crash of 1929 through the late 1930s. They learn that Ontario, as Canada's industrial heartland, was hit hard: manufacturing output collapsed, construction nearly halted, and urban unemployment reached roughly a quarter of the workforce by 1933, with industrial cities such as Hamilton and Windsor suffering even more. Students trace the human impact through meagre relief payments, soup kitchens, shantytowns such as Toronto's Don Flats, the humiliation of means tests, and the particular hardships of single unemployed men who were sent to transient relief camps far from their families. Key political topics include the premierships of G. Howard Ferguson and Mitchell Hepburn, the Hepburn government's open conflict with Prime Minister Mackenzie King over who should pay for relief, and the province's use of police against unemployed protesters. Students examine the protest movements of the decade, including the On-to-Ottawa Trek of 1935 and its violent end at Regina, the growth of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation as a socialist alternative, and Social Credit ideas arriving from western Canada. A central case study is the 1937 Oshawa General Motors strike, when autoworkers won recognition from the company while Premier Hepburn, despite his earlier sympathy for some workers, raised a volunteer police force to confront the union. Students also assess the longer-term legacy of the decade: the discrediting of laissez-faire economics, the pressure for unemployment insurance and social welfare programs that arrived with the war, and the uneven experience of farmers, women, immigrants, and Indigenous communities. Skills include reading unemployment and production statistics, comparing relief policies across municipalities, and judging whether the Depression in Ontario was caused more by global economic collapse or by domestic policy choices.
entries.pedagogicalNotes: Students often assume the Depression affected everyone equally. Contrast relief rates for single men, families, and farmers, and contrast industrial Windsor with a northern mining town. Build numeracy by having students read a simple unemployment or production graph before discussing causes. Keep the Oshawa strike discussion balanced: Hepburn's position appears contradictory to students, and working through that contradiction teaches that politicians respond to multiple pressures.

exampleProblems.problem: Describe two effects of the Great Depression on ordinary people in Ontario cities in the early 1930s.
exampleProblems.solution: Any two of: large-scale unemployment meant families could not pay rent and risked losing their homes; relief payments were very small and recipients faced humiliating means tests; unemployed single men were moved into federal relief camps doing manual labour for tiny wages; shantytowns built from scrap lumber appeared on the edges of cities; people moved in with relatives and marriage and birth rates fell.
exampleProblems.explanation: This easy question checks whether students can connect macroeconomic events to everyday experience. Strong answers give concrete conditions rather than simply repeating that times were hard.

exampleProblems.problem: Why did the 1937 Oshawa General Motors strike matter for the history of organized labour in Ontario?
exampleProblems.solution: Workers at the General Motors plant in Oshawa struck for union recognition, better wages, and shorter hours. The newly formed United Auto Workers, supported by the American-based Congress of Industrial Organizations, organized the walkout. Premier Mitchell Hepburn opposed the union and organized a volunteer police force to intervene, but the company eventually settled and recognized the union after about two weeks. The strike showed that industrial unions could win recognition in Ontario's auto sector, laid the groundwork for the powerful Canadian auto workers' unions of the postwar decades, and revealed that even a reform-minded premier could side with employers against organized labour.
exampleProblems.explanation: This medium question asks for significance, not just narrative. Students must explain why the event mattered later, connecting a single strike to the growth of industrial unionism in Ontario.

exampleProblems.problem: Assess the claim: 'The Great Depression in Ontario was caused mainly by government policy failures rather than by the collapse of the world economy.' Do you agree? Use specific evidence.
exampleProblems.solution: A strong answer takes a balanced position. Supporting evidence for the world economy: Ontario's prosperity depended on exports of wheat, minerals, newsprint, and manufactured goods, so the 1929 crash, falling world commodity prices, and American tariffs such as the Smoot-Hawley tariff of 1930 destroyed demand for Ontario products regardless of local policy. Supporting evidence for policy failure: the reliance on municipal and provincial relief rather than national unemployment insurance left people in poverty; the Hepburn government's conflicts with Ottawa delayed coordinated action; and police were used against protesters instead of addressing the causes of unemployment. A good conclusion argues that the trigger was external but that Canadian and Ontario policy choices made the suffering deeper and longer than it needed to be.
exampleProblems.explanation: This hard question requires weighing two explanations with evidence on both sides. Students practice building a qualified argument and learn that most historical outcomes have both structural causes and human decisions behind them.

entries.title: Grade 13 Ontario History: The Second World War, Postwar Immigration, and Urbanization
entries.contentBody: At the Grade 13 level students examine Ontario during the Second World War and the province's transformation in the first postwar decade. They learn that the war ended the Depression almost overnight: Ontario factories converted to munitions production, turning out military vehicles, aircraft, ships, and weapons under federal wartime direction, and unemployment virtually disappeared. Students study the wartime home front, including rationing of sugar, butter, gasoline, and rubber, Victory Bond campaigns, price controls, and the National Selective Service that directed workers to essential industries. They consider wartime social change, including women's mass entry into industrial work, the 1942 conscription plebiscite in which Ontario voted overwhelmingly in favour while Quebec did not, and the restrictive refugee policies that kept many European Jews from escaping to Canada before and during the war. Postwar topics include the baby boom, the acute housing shortage and the new suburban subdivisions rising around Toronto, Hamilton, and Windsor, the expansion of highways such as the Queen Elizabeth Way and Highway 401, and the construction of the St. Lawrence Seaway, which opened new shipping routes for Ontario industry. Students study mass immigration that reshaped the province: newcomers from Britain, Italy, Poland, the Netherlands, and other European countries arrived in large numbers to work in factories and build the cities, supported by agreements such as the one that brought Italian and Portuguese workers to Ontario. The 1947 Canadian Citizenship Act gave Canadians a citizenship of their own for the first time, and students discuss what belonging meant for new arrivals. Finally, the unit introduces the early Cold War in Ontario, including the 1945 Gouzenko affair in Ottawa that exposed Soviet espionage and began an era of security fears and political suspicion.
entries.pedagogicalNotes: Students frequently assume that wartime social gains were permanent; have them compare wartime wage-earning women with postwar expectations about women's work to test that assumption. Use photographs of wartime plants and postwar subdivisions to make urbanization visible. Map exercises showing where immigrant groups settled in Toronto, Hamilton, and Windsor help students see the geography of postwar change. Address the refugee record honestly: it is a key example of how policy choices affected people's survival.

exampleProblems.problem: Name two ways Ontario's economy changed during the Second World War.
exampleProblems.solution: Any two of: factories switched from consumer goods to weapons, vehicles, aircraft, and ships for the war effort; unemployment fell sharply because war production needed workers; women entered industrial jobs in large numbers; the government controlled prices, wages, and the distribution of scarce goods such as rubber and gasoline; federal agencies directed workers into essential industries.
exampleProblems.explanation: This easy question checks basic understanding that the war ended mass unemployment and reorganized industry. Good answers give specific examples of production rather than vague statements.

exampleProblems.problem: Explain how immigration and suburban growth changed Ontario cities between 1945 and the mid-1950s.
exampleProblems.solution: After 1945, Ontario needed workers for its expanding factories and faced a severe housing shortage. Large numbers of immigrants arrived from Britain, Italy, Poland, the Netherlands, and other European countries, and many took industrial jobs in Toronto, Hamilton, and Windsor. Highway construction and the growth of car ownership made it possible to build subdivisions on farmland outside the old city cores, so cities like Toronto expanded rapidly into suburbs such as North York, Scarborough, and Etobicoke. New schools, churches, and shopping plazas followed the population, and the ethnic mix of Ontario's cities became far more diverse than it had been in the 1930s.
exampleProblems.explanation: This medium question asks students to link two processes, immigration and urbanization, and explain how they reinforced each other rather than listing them separately.

exampleProblems.problem: Evaluate the statement: 'The Second World War improved life for everyone in Ontario equally.' Use evidence from at least two groups.
exampleProblems.solution: A strong answer rejects or heavily qualifies the claim. For some groups the war brought steady work, higher wages, and new opportunities, especially women in industry and men in the armed forces. For others it brought loss and injustice: soldiers and their families suffered casualties; Japanese Canadians were interned and lost property despite living mostly in British Columbia, showing how wartime fear targeted minorities; Indigenous veterans served but returned to unequal benefits and continued discrimination; and refugee policies excluded many who needed asylum. The war ended the Depression, but its benefits and burdens were distributed unevenly, which is the key judgement the evidence supports.
exampleProblems.explanation: This hard question trains students to test a sweeping generalization against the experience of specific groups, a core skill in social history and equity-focused analysis.

entries.title: Grade 14 Ontario History: The Auto Industry, Manufacturing, and the Postwar Economy
entries.contentBody: At the Grade 14 level students analyze the rise of Ontario's automobile industry and the manufacturing economy that shaped the province from the early twentieth century to the 1980s. They learn that Ontario's place in the North American auto industry rests on deep roots: early assembly plants such as Ford in Windsor and General Motors in Oshawa, the branch-plant strategy of American firms locating production in Canada, and the abundant steel from Hamilton's Stelco and Dofasco. The turning point for the modern industry is the 1965 Canada-United States Automotive Products Agreement, known as the Auto Pact, which removed tariffs on vehicles and parts between the two countries and integrated production across the border. Students see how this made plants in Windsor, Oshawa, Bramalea, Oakville, St. Thomas, and Kitchener-Waterloo's parts suppliers central to North American output, and how auto assembly became the backbone of the postwar middle class through high wages, pensions, and home ownership. Labour history runs through the unit: the 1937 Oshawa strike, the growth of the United Auto Workers, and the creation of the Canadian Auto Workers in 1985 after a split led by Bob White over how much the union should take direction from its American parent. Students also examine the risks of a branch-plant economy, including foreign ownership of major firms, a point raised by the 1957 Gordon Royal Commission on Canada's Economic Prospects. Economic concepts such as comparative advantage, economies of scale, and regional development policy are applied to the Ontario case. Students assess how recessions in the late 1950s, 1981 to 1982, and the early 1990s, together with automation and Japanese competition, tested the industry, and they study the 1988 federal election debate over free trade with the United States as a moment when Ontario's industrial future was at stake.
entries.pedagogicalNotes: Students often find economics abstract; anchor every concept in a real Ontario plant or community. A plant-to-community case study, such as Windsor and Chrysler or Oshawa and General Motors, makes dependency and layoffs concrete. Watch for the misconception that American branch plants were simply 'American factories in Canada'; explain the tariff and trade-policy reasons they existed. Keep the free-trade discussion structured with evidence from both sides so it does not become a partisan debate.

exampleProblems.problem: What was the Auto Pact of 1965 and why did it matter to Ontario?
exampleProblems.solution: The Automotive Products Agreement of 1965 removed tariffs on vehicles and auto parts traded between Canada and the United States, provided that manufacturers kept production and employment in Canada. For Ontario this meant that plants in Windsor, Oshawa, Oakville, and other cities became part of a single continental production system, and both output and employment in the auto sector grew enormously over the following two decades.
exampleProblems.explanation: This easy question checks a key factual turning point. Students should name the agreement, its date, and its effect on Ontario production.

exampleProblems.problem: Explain how Ontario's auto industry could both build the middle class and create economic risk for towns that depended on it.
exampleProblems.solution: Assembly plants and their parts suppliers offered steady, well-paid jobs with benefits, which allowed workers to buy homes and build stable communities, so towns like Oshawa, Windsor, and St. Thomas prospered. At the same time, those towns depended on decisions made in corporate head offices in the United States. When sales fell during recessions, or when companies restructured or automated production, layoffs hit the whole community because so many workers were in the same industry. The result was that the same plants that built prosperity also made towns vulnerable to outside economic decisions.
exampleProblems.explanation: This medium question asks students to see two sides of the same fact. The skill is connecting industrial structure to community outcomes rather than treating them as separate topics.

exampleProblems.problem: Assess the extent to which the 1965 Auto Pact made Ontario's manufacturing economy dependent on the United States. Use at least two forms of evidence in your answer.
exampleProblems.solution: A strong answer argues that the Auto Pact greatly deepened integration and dependency. Evidence one: production planning was coordinated from corporate head offices in Detroit and elsewhere, so Ontario plants built what the continental market needed, not necessarily what Canadian consumers wanted. Evidence two: employment and export figures show that Ontario's auto output was overwhelmingly destined for the United States, so American recessions and trade disputes transmitted directly into Ontario job losses, as in 1981 to 1982 and the early 1990s. Evidence for partial independence: the pact's Canadian value-added requirements preserved a large parts sector and tens of thousands of jobs, and Ontario's steel and machinery industries grew alongside it. A balanced conclusion holds that the pact brought enormous prosperity but at the cost of tying Ontario's economic fortunes closely to American demand and American corporate decisions.
exampleProblems.explanation: This hard question requires a judgement supported by trade and employment evidence and a counterargument. It teaches students to evaluate a policy by its long-term structural effects, not just its immediate benefits.

entries.title: Grade 15 Ontario History: Postwar Politics from Robarts to Harris and Economic Change
entries.contentBody: At the Grade 15 level students study Ontario politics from the early 1960s to the late 1990s alongside the province's economic transformation. The unit begins with the long Progressive Conservative dynasty: John Robarts as premier from 1961 to 1971 presided over an affluent, confident Ontario, expanding universities and highways and presenting the province as the national engine of growth. His successor Bill Davis, premier from 1971 to 1985, is remembered as the education premier: he expanded the public school system, created the community college system in 1967, founded TVOntario in 1970, extended full public funding to Catholic secondary schools in 1984, and supported the new Canadian constitution and Charter of Rights in the 1981 patriation negotiations. Students then examine the end of the Tory era: David Peterson's Liberals governed from 1985 with NDP support, and in 1990 Bob Rae's New Democrats formed government amid a recession. The Rae years are studied through the 1993 Social Contract, which imposed unpaid days off for public servants, known as Rae Days, to avoid layoffs during a severe deficit. Students evaluate that policy neutrally: supporters argued it saved jobs and protected public services, while critics on both the left and the right argued it broke promises or unfairly burdened workers. In 1995 Mike Harris's Progressive Conservatives won on the Common Sense Revolution platform, promising major tax cuts, reduced welfare rates, fewer regulations, and smaller government. Students examine in neutral terms the Harris government's key measures: the Common Sense Revolution itself, the 1998 amalgamation of Toronto and its suburbs into a single city, the leasing of the privately operated Highway 407, the downloading of service costs to municipalities, the 1996 teachers' strikes and public protests, and the 1995 Ipperwash occupation and the death of Dudley George. The unit links politics to economic change: Ontario's shift from manufacturing toward finance, services, and technology, the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement, and debates over electricity restructuring and the future of Ontario Hydro.
entries.pedagogicalNotes: This material is politically sensitive and recent enough that students arrive with family opinions. Set a firm rule of describing each government's goals, evidence, and the arguments of both supporters and critics in neutral terms. Common misconceptions: that Rae Days were 'days off work' with no purpose, and that the Harris reforms simply cut services without any stated fiscal rationale. Use policy documents and newspaper editorials from the period rather than retrospective opinion pieces, and anchor abstract fiscal debates in concrete examples like school funding or municipal budgets.

exampleProblems.problem: Identify two policies of the Harris government elected in 1995 and state the goal of each.
exampleProblems.solution: Any two of: the Common Sense Revolution promised large personal income tax cuts and lower business taxes to stimulate growth; welfare rates were cut by about 20 percent to reduce spending and discourage long-term dependence; the six Toronto-area municipalities were amalgamated into one city in 1998 to cut administrative duplication; the Highway 407 was leased to a private operator to raise revenue and shift operations to the private sector; some service costs were downloaded from the province to municipalities to balance the provincial budget.
exampleProblems.explanation: This easy question checks factual recall. The second half of the question, stating the goal, pushes students to see that every policy has a stated purpose, which is the first step toward neutral evaluation.

exampleProblems.problem: Explain what the 'Rae Days' were and why they were controversial.
exampleProblems.solution: In 1993 the NDP government of Bob Rae faced a large deficit during a recession. The Social Contract required most public servants to take twelve unpaid days off per year, rather than laying off workers or cutting services outright. Supporters said the measure saved tens of thousands of jobs and protected public services in a crisis. Critics on the left said the government had broken its promise not to attack workers' collective agreements, while critics on the right argued that the measure shielded the public service from the spending cuts everyone else faced. The policy became a defining symbol of the Rae government and of the difficulties of governing during a fiscal crisis.
exampleProblems.explanation: This medium question requires both description and explanation of controversy. Students must present both sides before any judgement, which is the discipline this unit is built around.

exampleProblems.problem: Compare the approaches of the Davis governments of the 1970s and the Harris governments of the late 1990s to the role of the provincial state. What remained constant even as the philosophy changed?
exampleProblems.solution: A strong answer contrasts the two eras. Davis expanded the state's role in education, created institutions such as TVOntario and the community colleges, and generally managed growth with regulation and public investment, earning a reputation for pragmatic centrism. Harris argued that government was too large and expensive, cut taxes and welfare rates, amalgamated Toronto, leased the 407, and pushed the private sector into areas the province had managed. What remained constant was that both governments used provincial power actively to shape the economy and society: neither was truly laissez-faire. Davis built institutions while Harris restructured them, and both acted decisively in education, which remained a provincial responsibility at the heart of Ontario politics. The comparison shows that the debate was about the means and scope of government, not about whether government should act at all.
exampleProblems.explanation: This hard comparison question asks students to identify both difference and continuity across two governments, the core analytic move in political history. It also models how to treat both eras on the same neutral terms.

entries.title: Grade 16 Ontario History: Indigenous Treaties, Land Claims, and Reconciliation
entries.contentBody: At the Grade 16 level students study the history of treaties and land claims involving First Nations in Ontario, and they learn that treaty making is the foundation of the relationship between Indigenous peoples and the Crown. The legal starting point is the Royal Proclamation of 1763, which declared that Indigenous lands could be surrendered only to the Crown through formal agreements, a principle still recognized in section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982. Students survey the treaties covering Ontario: early agreements such as those surrounding the 1764 Treaty of Niagara, the Huron Tract treaties of the 1820s, the 1850 Robinson-Huron and Robinson-Superior Treaties signed at Sault Ste. Marie, the 1923 Williams Treaties on Lake Ontario and Lake Simcoe, and the numbered treaties of the north, including Treaty 3, Treaty 5, Treaty 9, and the treaty extensions of 1905 to 1906 and 1929 to 1930. The unit teaches students to hold two perspectives together: the Crown historically treated many treaties as surrenders of land for cash and reserves, while First Nations understand the same agreements as sharing the land, keeping their way of life, and building an ongoing relationship. Contemporary cases make the stakes clear. The 2018 Supreme Court of Canada decision in Restoule confirmed that annuity payments under the Robinson treaties must be augmented, reflecting the promise in those agreements. The Williams Treaties communities' harvesting claims, the long struggle of Grassy Narrows over mercury contamination of the Wabigoon River from a Dryden mill, and the 1995 occupation at Ipperwash that ended with the death of Dudley George all show how unresolved land and rights issues persist. Students also examine the numbered treaties' promises concerning education, hunting, and annuities, the residential school system and its survivors, including institutions such as St. Anne's in Fort Albany and the Shingwauk school in Sault Ste. Marie, and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's Calls to Action as a framework for Ontario classrooms and institutions today.
entries.pedagogicalNotes: The most common misconception is that treaties are historical artifacts rather than living agreements. Counter it by pairing each treaty text with a current court decision or land claim. Avoid presenting the whole subject as one of grievance: emphasize First Nations agency, diplomacy, and the diversity of communities and positions. Teach the vocabulary of treaty, reserve, surrender, and annuity explicitly before reading documents, and be prepared for students' questions about their own communities and family histories with local resources.

exampleProblems.problem: What did the Royal Proclamation of 1763 say about Indigenous lands, and why does it still matter?
exampleProblems.solution: The Royal Proclamation declared that Indigenous peoples held rights to their lands and that those lands could be surrendered only to the Crown through formal agreements, not taken by private individuals or settlers on their own authority. It still matters because courts treat it as the origin of the duty to negotiate treaties, and section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982 recognizes and affirms existing Aboriginal and treaty rights, so the principle continues to shape land claims and resource development in Ontario.
exampleProblems.explanation: This easy question checks a foundational legal fact and its continuing relevance, which is the anchor for the whole unit.

exampleProblems.problem: Explain how the Robinson-Huron Treaty of 1850 illustrates the two different understandings of treaties.
exampleProblems.solution: The treaty was negotiated at Sault Ste. Marie between the Crown and the Anishinaabe of the upper Great Lakes region. The Crown recorded it as a surrender of the land in exchange for reserves and annual cash payments, called annuities. The First Nations signatories understood that they were sharing the land and its resources with the newcomers while continuing their own way of life, and that the Crown's wealth from the land meant the annuities would grow over time. The dispute over whether annuities had to be augmented as revenues grew went to the Supreme Court of Canada, which in 2018 confirmed that the treaty relationship required the payments to be increased, showing that the two understandings are still being reconciled today.
exampleProblems.explanation: This medium question asks students to see the same document from two perspectives, the central skill in treaty studies, and to connect a nineteenth-century agreement to a modern court decision.

exampleProblems.problem: Evaluate the statement: 'Residential schools and treaty relationships are separate issues in Ontario history.' Do you agree? Use evidence.
exampleProblems.solution: A strong answer disagrees and shows the connections. Many treaties included promises about education, and the federal government used those clauses to justify the residential school system, including St. Anne's School in Fort Albany and the Shingwauk institution in Sault Ste. Marie. The schools' purpose of assimilation contradicted the treaties' understanding of sharing the land while maintaining Indigenous ways of life, and the intergenerational harms of the schools affect the capacity of communities to engage with land and governance issues today. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission treated treaty relationships and the schools as parts of the same history, and its Calls to Action address education, language, and land as connected matters. A good conclusion recognizes that the issues are distinct in some legal terms but inseparable in the lived history of Ontario First Nations.
exampleProblems.explanation: This hard question asks students to test a claim about the relationship between two historical topics. It builds the ability to synthesize across a unit and to argue with evidence from law, education, and community experience.

entries.title: Grade 17 Ontario History: Immigration and Multiculturalism in Toronto, Greenbelt, and Algonquin
entries.contentBody: At the Grade 17 level students examine two connected themes: the making of multicultural Toronto and Ontario's environmental history. On the first theme, students learn that Toronto's population was transformed after 1945 by successive waves of immigration. The 1947 Canadian Citizenship Act created a distinct Canadian citizenship, and the 1967 points system replaced older preferences for British and European immigrants with largely non-discriminatory selection based on skills and education. Students trace the arrival of postwar European newcomers, the 1956 Hungarian refugees, Ugandan Asians in 1972, and growing migration from Hong Kong and mainland China, the Philippines, India and Punjab, Sri Lanka, Portugal, Italy, and Jamaica and the Caribbean.
